01.note: Members of a wedding party wanted to bring water in on Shabbat from a public area into a private one, and they did it by lining up the many people present as a wall, with the people knowing they were being used that way. Shmuel ordered the wedding party to be flogged. He asked: if the Sages allowed a human wall when the people do not know what they are being used for, does that mean they would allow it when the people know?
01.why: The Gemara has just drawn a line between people who serve as a wall knowingly, which is forbidden, and unknowingly, which is allowed. Shmuel's punishment of the wedding party shows the forbidden side of that line in practice.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who ordered the wedding party flogged for using people knowingly as a wall.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, on which carrying objects from a public area into a private one is forbidden.
A wall or barrier that changes the legal status of an area for carrying on Shabbat. Here the 'wall' is made of standing people.
Whipped as a punishment imposed by the Sages for breaking their rules.

02.note: Some flasks were lying in the marketplace of Mehoza on Shabbat, where they could not be moved. When Rava came back from giving his public lecture, a crowd walked with him, and his attendants used the crowd as a human wall to carry the flasks into his house. On another Shabbat they wanted to do the same thing, but Rava forbade it: this time the people would know what they were being used for, and that is forbidden.
02.why: The discussion has drawn a line between people who unknowingly serve as a wall, which is allowed, and those who knowingly do, which is forbidden. Rava's two Shabbats show the same act landing on both sides of that line.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage returning from his lecture; his attendants used the crowd around him to bring the flasks into his house.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, on which carrying objects from a public area into a private one is forbidden.
A town in Babylonia, where Rava lived.
A row of people treated as a wall, which can make carrying on Shabbat permitted in certain cases.

03.note: Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, explains that those who go out to save lives on Shabbat may come home carrying their weapons, and cites an old teaching about how this came about. At first, defenders returning from a rescue would leave their weapons in the first house by the town wall. Once, enemies noticed they were unarmed and chased them; the defenders rushed into the house for their weapons, the enemies followed them in, and in the crush they killed more of each other than the enemies killed. After that the Sages ruled that defenders return to their places with their weapons.
03.why: The Gemara asked whether rescuers may walk home more than the usual two thousand cubits on Shabbat. Rav's answer reads the permission as being about carrying weapons home, and this disaster explains why that permission was given.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Sage who reports Rav's explanation and the old teaching behind it.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose explanation Rav Yehuda quotes.

terms.meaning: A collection of early rabbinic teachings, from the same period as the Mishna, quoted here as the source of the story.
The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, on which carrying and walking far are restricted, though saving lives overrides these rules.

04.note: Rabbi Yehuda tells of Rabbi Tarfon, who was traveling on the eve of Shabbat when night fell, so he spent the night outside a town. In the morning, cowherds found him and said: Master, the town is right in front of you, go in. He went in, sat in the study hall, and taught all day.
04.why: The Mishna records a dispute: Rabbi Meir says a traveler who did not mean to settle near a town may not enter it on Shabbat; Rabbi Yehuda says he may, citing Rabbi Tarfon. The other Sages reply that Tarfon may have intended it, or the study hall was within his limit.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A Sage who slept outside a town on Shabbat and entered it in the morning when cowherds urged him to.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who tells the story about Rabbi Tarfon.

terms.meaning: On Shabbat a person may walk only about two thousand cubits (roughly a kilometer) from where he was when Shabbat began; a town may lie inside or outside that range.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the main collection of their rulings.
The house where the Sages and their students gathered to learn and teach Torah.

05.note: Rabbi Yosei reports that Yosef the priest left the Land of Israel and went to his teacher in Tzeidan, outside the land, to learn Torah. The translation adds that the leading Sage of the time, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, was living in the Land of Israel.
05.why: The question is whether a priest may leave the Land of Israel, and become ritually impure, to study Torah when there is a teacher at home. Rabbi Yosei says yes, since not everyone can learn from every teacher, and cites Yosef the priest. Rabbi Yohanan rules like Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Yosef the priest
people.about: A priest who went to his teacher in Tzeidan, outside the Land of Israel, to study Torah.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who tells about Yosef the priest to support his view.

terms.meaning: A descendant of Aaron (a kohen). Priests must avoid ritual impurity, and the Sages treated lands outside Israel as impure.
Sidon, a city on the coast north of the Land of Israel.

05.flag: Very short: only the bare report that Yosef the priest went to Tzeidan, with no further events.

06.note: Rams were brought on Shabbat to the town of Mavrakhta, and Rava allowed the people of Mehoza to buy them and take them home. Ravina challenged him: you must be relying on Shmuel, who said a gentile's property is not tied to a Shabbat location, but the law follows Rabbi Yohanan, who said it is. Rava changed his ruling: the rams could be sold only to the people of Mavrakhta itself, since for them the whole town counts as the animals' own small area.
06.why: The Gemara has just set out the dispute over whether objects owned by a gentile are fixed to a Shabbat location, with Rabbi Yohanan saying they are. The case of the rams shows the dispute decided in practice in Rabbi Yohanan's favor.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who first let the people of Mehoza buy the rams, then took back that ruling.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Sage who challenged Rava's ruling.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage cited for the view that a gentile's property does not acquire a Shabbat location.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage cited for the view that it does; the law follows him.

terms.meaning: When Shabbat begins, people and objects become tied to where they are and may be moved only within a set range of that spot.
The small area, about two meters, within which something outside its permitted range may still be moved on Shabbat.
The distance, two thousand cubits, beyond a town that a person may walk on Shabbat.

07.note: Rav Mesharshiya gave his son a question to ask Rav Pappa: are a person's four cubits on Shabbat measured by his own forearm, or by the standard measure? He even prepared the follow-up challenges for either answer, including what to do about the giant Og, king of Bashan. When the son asked, Rav Pappa answered that if we were that precise we could never study anything. He then ruled that each person's own forearm is the measure, and explained why the rule was left off the list of measures that vary from person to person: some people have short limbs for their bodies.
07.why: The Gemara has been asking where the four cubits a person may always move within on Shabbat come from and how big they are. Rav Mesharshiya's question pushes on exactly how they are measured.

people.name: Rav Mesharshiya
people.about: Sage who sent his son with a question for Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who answered the question.

people.name: Og, king of the Bashan
people.about: A giant king from the Bible, raised as a test case for the measurement.

terms.meaning: A unit of length based on the forearm, from elbow to fingertip, roughly half a meter.
A fixed, standard cubit used in Temple matters, the same for everyone.
The small area around a person in which he may always move on Shabbat, even when he may not walk anywhere else.

08.note: Rabbi Yehuda tells of the households of Memel and Guryon in the village of Aroma, who handed out dried figs and raisins to the poor in years of famine. The poor of the villages of Sihin and Hananya would walk to the edge of their Shabbat limit by nightfall on Friday, and early the next morning they would set off and come to collect the food.
08.why: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree over who may fix his Shabbat base far from home just by standing there. Rabbi Yehuda says even someone with a home and food may, and cites the paupers walking to Aroma as precedent.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who tells the story to support his view.

people.name: Memel and Guryon households
people.about: Families in Aroma who gave figs and raisins to the poor during famine.

terms.meaning: A legal device that lets a person on Shabbat walk further than usual by fixing his base at another spot, either by placing food there or by standing there.
The distance, two thousand cubits, a person may walk beyond his town on Shabbat.

09.note: Rabba bar Rav Hanan used to walk on Shabbat from his home in Artibbena to Pumbedita, and to do it he would declare from home on Friday: my Shabbat base is in Tzinta, a place between the two. Abaye challenged him: you are relying on Rabbi Yehuda as Rav Hisda explained him, but Rav Nahman explained the dispute differently, and a teaching supports Rav Nahman. Rabba bar Rav Hanan said: I take back my view.
09.why: Rav has just ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, who lets even a person at home fix his base elsewhere. Rabba bar Rav Hanan acted on a wide reading of that, and Abaye uses Rav Nahman's reading, backed by a baraita, to show it does not reach so far.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Hanan
people.about: Sage who walked on Shabbat from Artibbena to Pumbedita by declaring his base in Tzinta.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who challenged his practice.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Sage whose explanation of the dispute Rabba bar Rav Hanan relied on.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage who explained the dispute differently, in a way that rules out the practice.

terms.meaning: A spoken declaration that fixes a person's Shabbat base at a spot other than his home, so he can walk two thousand cubits from there.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

10.note: Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata brought a basket of fruit on the eve of Shabbat to Rav Natan bar Oshaya, who lived in another town. As he was leaving, Rav Natan let him go down one step and then said: stay here tonight. The next morning Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata rose early and walked home. The Gemara asks which Sages' views Rav Natan's action followed, and gives two possible answers.
10.why: The Gemara has been working out Ulla's ruling that a man who set out on his journey and was then persuaded to turn back still counts as having set out. Rav Natan's move, letting his guest start out before asking him to stay, looks like that ruling in action.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata
people.about: Sage who brought fruit to Rav Natan bar Oshaya and stayed the night.

people.name: Rav Natan bar Oshaya
people.about: The host who let his guest step out before asking him to stay.

terms.meaning: Having actually started a journey before Shabbat, which can let a traveler fix his Shabbat base along the road and so reach home the next day.

11.note: A woman came before a judge meaning to say: Master, sir, I had a board and it was stolen from me. Because she mispronounced her words, what she actually said was: Master, servant, I had a beam and they stole you from me, and it was so big that when they hung you on it your feet did not reach the ground.
11.why: The Gemara is contrasting the precise speech of the people of Judea with the careless speech of Galileans, and this is one of several examples of Galileans whose mispronunciation turned their words into nonsense or insult.

terms.meaning: People of the Galilee, in northern Israel, whose speech the Gemara describes here as imprecise, especially in pronouncing certain letters.

12.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya said that no one ever got the better of him in words except a woman, a young boy and a young girl. The woman was his hostess at an inn. She served him beans, and the first two days he ate them all without leaving any on his plate. On the third day she over-salted them, and he stopped eating. When she asked why, he politely said he had already eaten during the day; she said he should have held back from bread then, and asked whether he was now leaving food because he had not left any the first days, as the Sages say a guest should leave some on the plate.
12.why: The Gemara has been collecting examples of clever and witty speech, and this is the first of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya's three tales of being outwitted.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage who tells of the few times he was beaten in a verbal exchange.

people.name: the hostess
people.about: The woman who ran the inn where he stayed and who over-salted his beans.

terms.meaning: Good manners of the time: a guest left a little food on his plate rather than clearing it.

13.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya tells how a young girl got the better of him. He was walking along a path that crossed a field, and a girl said to him: Rabbi, isn't this a field? He answered that it was a well-trodden path. She said: robbers like you have trodden it.
13.why: This is the second of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya's three tales of being beaten in words, after the hostess and before the young boy, in a run of stories about clever speech.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage who tells of the times he was outwitted.

people.name: a young girl
people.about: The girl who rebuked him for walking through a field.

terms.meaning: A path already beaten through a field, where walking does no further harm to crops and so is allowed.

14.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya tells how a young boy got the better of him. He met the boy at a crossroads and asked the way to the city. The boy said one road was short and long, the other long and short. He took the short-and-long road, but near the city found it ringed by gardens and orchards he could not get through. He went back and said: my son, didn't you tell me this way was short? The boy answered: and didn't I tell you it was long? He kissed the boy on the head and said: happy are you, Israel, for you are all very wise, from old to young.
14.why: This is the third of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya's three tales of being beaten in words, in a run of stories about clever speech.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage who tells of the times he was outwitted.

people.name: a young boy
people.about: The boy at the crossroads who gave him a riddling answer about the way to the city.

15.note: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili was walking along the road when he met Berurya, and asked her: by which road shall we go to Lod? She answered: foolish Galilean, didn't the Sages say, do not talk much with a woman? You should have said: which way to Lod?
15.why: The Gemara has been telling stories of clever speech and of the wisdom of women; Berurya's retort follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya's tales and uses the familiar jibe at Galileans' wordiness.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
people.about: A Sage from the Galilee who asked Berurya the way to Lod.

people.name: Berurya
people.about: A learned woman who mocked his wordy question.

terms.meaning: Someone from the Galilee in northern Israel; the discussion has been teasing Galileans for careless speech.
A town in the Land of Israel, also known as Lydda.

16.note: Berurya came across a student who was whispering his studies instead of saying them aloud. She kicked him and quoted the verse 'ordered in all things and secure': if the Torah is set in all of your 248 limbs, it stays with you, and if not, it does not. The Gemara adds a teaching that Rabbi Eliezer had a student who studied quietly and after three years forgot what he had learned.
16.why: This follows another story of Berurya's wit, and leads into Shmuel's advice to Rav Yehuda to open his mouth when he studies so that his learning lasts.

people.name: Berurya
people.about: A learned woman who kicked a student for studying in a whisper.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage whose quiet-studying student forgot his learning after three years.

terms.meaning: The traditional count of the parts of the human body; here it means studying with the whole body, aloud.

17.note: Rav Yosef held a grievance against Rava. On the eve of Yom Kippur Rava decided to go and make peace with him. He found Rav Yosef's attendant mixing him a cup of wine, took the cup and mixed it himself. Rav Yosef, who was blind, tasted it and said it was like Rava's mixing; Rava said: it is I. Rav Yosef told him not to sit down until he explained the verses about the journey from the wilderness to Mattanah, Nahaliel, Bamoth and the valley. Rava explained: a person who makes himself humble like the wilderness receives the Torah as a gift and rises to greatness; if he grows proud, God brings him low, and if he repents, God raises him again.
17.why: Rav Mattana has just read the same verse, 'from the wilderness to Mattanah', as teaching that Torah lasts only for the humble. The story carries that teaching further, in a scene that is itself about Rava humbling himself.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Son of Rav Yosef bar Hama; went to make peace with Rav Yosef on the eve of Yom Kippur.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A blind Sage who had a grievance against Rava.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement; on its eve people seek forgiveness from anyone they have wronged.
Wine was then strong and was mixed with water before drinking; each person's mixing could be recognized by taste.
Places on the Israelites' route in the Book of Numbers; their names sound like the Hebrew for gift, God's inheritance, and heights.

18.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was so absorbed in Torah study that he would sit learning in the lower market of Tzippori while his cloak lay in the upper market. Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elazar reported that once a man came to take the cloak and found a serpent on it.
18.why: The Gemara is reading the verse 'be you ravished always with her love' as praise for love of Torah that makes a person forget the world, and Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat is given as the example.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat
people.about: A Sage so lost in study that he left his cloak in another part of the market.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elazar
people.about: Sage who reports what happened when a man tried to take the cloak.

terms.meaning: A town in the Galilee with an upper and a lower marketplace.

19.note: Rabbi Perida had a student who needed every lesson taught four hundred times before he learned it. One day Rabbi Perida was called to a mitzva after the lesson, and this time four hundred repetitions were not enough. The student explained that once he heard his teacher was needed elsewhere, he kept thinking, now the master will get up and go. Rabbi Perida told him to pay attention and taught him another four hundred times. A Divine Voice then asked Rabbi Perida whether he would rather have four hundred years added to his life, or that he and his generation merit the World-to-Come. He chose the World-to-Come, and God said: give him both.
19.why: The discussion has turned to how Torah is learned and reviewed, with Moses teaching the Torah to everyone directly; Rabbi Perida's patience is the Gemara's example of repetition taken to the extreme.

people.name: Rabbi Perida
people.about: A Sage who taught a slow student each lesson four hundred times.

people.name: the student
people.about: Rabbi Perida's student, who needed four hundred repetitions to learn.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who grants Rabbi Perida both rewards.

terms.meaning: A religious duty, such as a communal obligation, for which Rabbi Perida's presence was requested.
A voice from heaven, the Gemara's way of describing a message from God.
The reward of the righteous after this life.

20.note: Residents of the city of Kakunya came to Rav Yosef and asked for someone to set up an eiruv for their city. Rav Yosef sent Abaye, telling him to make sure no one in the study hall could object to it. Abaye saw some houses that opened onto the river and not onto the city, and said: let these be the section left out of the eiruv. The story here ends there; what Abaye decided in the end is not part of it.
20.why: The Gemara is discussing how an eiruv is set up for a city, where the rule is that part of it must be left out. Abaye's visit to Kakunya tests what may count as that left-out part.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage the people of Kakunya asked for help; he sent Abaye.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rav Yosef's student, sent to set up the eiruv.

terms.meaning: A legal arrangement that joins the homes of a town or courtyard so that carrying among them is permitted on Shabbat.
For a city that was once public, the Sages required that part of it be left out of the eiruv as a reminder; this part is called the excluded section.
The house where the Sages studied, where a flawed ruling would be openly criticized.

20.flag: The story stops at Abaye's first decision; his retractions and final ruling, which follow at once in the next segments, are left outside the story.
